path: Horwath weighs her future while Loomis campaigns on taxes and competence, courting suburban voters; another centre-right figure considers entering the race.
A second conservative-leaning candidate enters, splitting the anti-incumbent vote; Horwath runs on incumbency and union support, defending strong-mayor use.
Low turnout favours organized bases; Horwath or a split field edges Loomis, who wins wards in Stoney Creek and Ancaster but not citywide.
Hostilities simmer; insurers keep Hormuz on listed areas and daily transits stay well below normal, with harassment incidents persisting.
US pressure and Gulf lobbying produce talks; a partial de-escalation lifts traffic, but a fresh incident spooks shipowners and pauses recovery.
Without several incident-free weeks, insurers stay cautious; 7-day average climbs toward but mostly below 60 by end of October.
US envoys push Beirut on disarmament timelines and convene the Naqoura mechanism; Israel keeps striking while attending.
Lebanon sends its civilian envoy to a session to press for withdrawal; Hezbollah denounces it but does not topple the cabinet.
A mechanism meeting with both delegations present occurs before August 31 and is reported, unless an escalation suspends sessions.
Congressional UAP caucus demands videos; AARO promises releases but works slowly through classification review.
ODNI focuses on other declassification priorities; a hearing prompts promises rather than a new document dump.
No clearly new UAP records are released before mid-September; a small AARO case release remains possible.
Linke surges among young voters, drawing from Greens; Greens poll around 14-15% and fight for inner-city direct seats.
CDU leads; BSW and FDP hover at threshold. Greens campaign on rents and transport but momentum stays with Linke.
Greens finish near 14-16%, translating to roughly 22-28 seats even with compensation, well short of 35.
Wegner campaigns on security; CDU polls 22-25% while Linke and AfD contest eastern direct seats.
Federal Merz unpopularity drags somewhat; AfD and Linke take several eastern constituencies, cutting CDU overhang.
CDU wins first place near 24% with around 35-42 direct mandates; total seats likely land below 45.
Andersson's S leads polls around 33-35%; SD and M campaign hard on crime to peel working-class voters.
Some erosion to V and SD; polls tighten slightly but S remains clearly above its 2022 result.
S finishes around 32-34%, yielding roughly 115-120 seats; falling under 105 needs a large polling miss.
Democrats target Kean in NJ-7 and defend NJ-9; midterm mood favours the party out of power.
Kean distances from Trump on SALT and tariffs; Democratic challenger gains on fundraising, NJ-9 Hispanic voters drift back.
Democrats hold all nine and narrowly flip NJ-7 for ten; Van Drew holds NJ-2 unless a big wave.
Democrats push IA-1 and IA-3 with farm-economy messaging; open IA-2 gets less investment.
Rob Sand's campaign lifts turnout; Miller-Meeks race tightens, Nunn holds a modest lead, IA-2 leans Republican.
Democrats flip at most one or two seats; winning three requires a wave Iowa's partisanship resists.
Redistricting amendment fights through courts and referendum; Republicans litigate procedural defects to force the old map.
Outcome of map litigation decides the landscape; if the new map stands, Democrats field candidates in redrawn seats.
With new map in a favourable midterm, Democrats win 9-10; under the old map they win about 7. Map uncertainty dominates.
Democrats target open AZ-1 and Ciscomani's AZ-6; Republican AZ-1 primary produces a more MAGA nominee.
Midterm independents sour on the president's party; AZ-1 tilts Democratic, Ciscomani leans on moderate brand.
Democrats likely flip AZ-1 but Ciscomani narrowly survives; both flips together happen only in a strong wave.
Democrats target Barrett in MI-7 and open MI-10, defend MI-8 and MI-3; Duggan independent run complicates turnout.
Tariff-related auto anxiety hurts Republicans; MI-7 leans Democratic, MI-10 tossup, MI-4 stays Republican.
Democrats flip one or two for 7-8 seats; a third flip needed for nine requires a wave plus holding MI-8.
Democrats target Mackenzie, Bresnahan and Perry; Fitzpatrick runs ahead of his party in PA-1.
Shapiro's strong re-election campaign boosts turnout; Bresnahan stock-trading attacks land.
Democrats flip two or three seats reaching 9-10; Fitzpatrick survives, so exactly 11 is unlikely.
Sand runs a rural-focused moderate campaign and raises heavily; Feenstra leans on Trump endorsement; Hinson leads the Senate race.
Farm economy pain narrows the governor race to near even while Hinson keeps a steady lead.
Ticket-splitting is plausible, but Iowa partisanship likely lets Feenstra edge Sand; Hinson wins comfortably.
Democratic Senate nominee challenges Collins in a favourable midterm; crowded gubernatorial field consolidates around the primary winner.
Collins runs on independence and outperforms polls in rural Maine; an independent governor candidate draws votes.
Democrats likely hold the governorship; Senate is close, with ranked-choice helping the Democrat. Both needed for sweep.
Brown runs a populist campaign ahead of party; Ramaswamy uses money and Trump endorsement against Acton.
Midterm mood tightens both races; Husted attacked over FirstEnergy ties but Ohio partisanship holds.
Brown has a real chance, Acton less so; Ramaswamy likely wins, preventing a Democratic sweep.
Election night shows a close count with Crowley narrowly ahead; runner-up waits for the county canvass.
Canvass moves totals by small amounts; runner-up weighs a recount but considers party unity against Tiffany.
Official margin stays narrow; whether Crowley's lead sits under 1% hinges on the close election-night figure, which the bracket framing suggests.
Crowley leads narrowly on election night; campaigns await canvass results across counties.
County canvasses correct small reporting errors, moving the margin by tenths of a point.
Certified margin must fall in a narrow 0.2-point band; even with a close race, exact bracket placement is uncertain.
All Okinawa coalition decides on Tamaki's third-term bid; LDP fields a challenger stressing economy and Tokyo funds.
Komeito's stance matters; economic concerns compete with Henoko opposition, while the coalition's recent losses weaken its machine.
Tamaki, if running, faces a close race against a better-organized conservative side; he may lose or not run.
Fragmented Chiclayo field of many lists; JEE reviews candidacies while crime and extortion dominate debate.
Polls show shifting leaders and late surges; corruption allegations hit some frontrunners.
Plurality winner emerges with 20-30%; with no evidence Gamarra leads, he is one of many contenders.
Many lists compete in Piura; candidates campaign on flooding, infrastructure and crime.
Late polls reshuffle the order; eligibility exclusions and scandals possible.
A plurality winner with roughly a quarter of votes emerges; Cueva Celi is one candidate among many without a known lead.
V polls 7-8%, clearly ahead of C, KD and MP; Dadgostar demands influence in an S-led government.
Some tactical drift from V to S as Andersson frames a two-way choice, but mid-size parties stay near 5-6%.
V finishes fourth in seats, comfortably ahead of the 5-6% parties.
KD, C and MP poll within a point of each other around 5-6%.
Moderate voters tactically support KD; Centre struggles after leadership churn; Greens mobilize youth weakly.
Order among the three is nearly random; MP finishes sixth in roughly one of three scenarios.
Liberals poll around 3%; Mohamsson fights for survival while internal splits over SD persist.
Moderates hint at support votes only if L is close; L stays below 4% in most final polls.
Some tactical help arrives but L likely ends just under 4%, winning no seats.
S leads with 33-35%; SD and V attack from both sides.
Campaign tightens modestly; no major S scandal emerges.
S finishes around 31-34%; dropping below 27% would need an unprecedented collapse.
Kristersson campaigns on economic recovery and tax cuts; M polls 17-19%.
Tactical support votes for KD and L drain M voters; SD competes for right-leaning votes.
M finishes around 18-19%; reaching 20% needs a late rally or polling miss.
V polls 7-8%; Dadgostar pushes for cabinet seats.
S frames election as Andersson vs Kristersson, prompting some tactical drift to S.
V lands near 7%; result between 5% and 7% is plausible if the squeeze bites, but polls point slightly above.
MP polls 5-6% with climate low on the agenda.
V and S compete for progressive young voters; no climate event lifts salience.
MP finishes around 5-6%; 7% or more would require a rare outperformance.
Centre polls 4-6% after leadership churn; Thand Ringqvist courts liberal voters.
Some Liberal voters move to C, but tactical votes flow to L and KD instead.
C ends near 5-6%; 7% or more needs a revival above its 2022 level.
Leavitt continues or returns after leave; deputies handle briefings as needed.
Trump keeps Leavitt or relies on internal deputies; Jennings stays at CNN.
No permanent successor announced by early October; if one is, an insider is likelier than Jennings.
